# What does a domain query measure?

[Predict the coordinates before you run the code.]{.lesson-deck}
:::

A helper name is not a substitute for its mathematical definition. OpenPFC
can report a domain's point count, dimensionality, bounds, extent and
`physical_volume`. These quantities answer related but different questions.

## Read the definitions

For size $(N_x,N_y,N_z)$, `get_total_size` counts $N_xN_yN_z$ samples.
`extent` subtracts `lower` from `upper`, respecting each axis's endpoint
convention. `physical_volume` uses the historical grid measure

$$V_h=N_xN_yN_z h_xh_yh_z.$$

On a fully periodic grid it equals the product of the extents. On a
nonperiodic axis, the stored coordinate span is $(N_x-1)h_x$, so those
products differ. This function does not introduce endpoint quadrature
weights or compute a physical integral of a field.

```{.cpp include="model.cpp" snippet="queries" dedent=2}
```

Here both grids have 30 points and `physical_volume=90`. Making x
nonperiodic changes its span from 2.5 to 2, and the product of the three
coordinate spans from 90 to 72. Nothing has changed the stored sample count.

## Ask for the quantity you need

```sh
openpfc run model.cpp input.json --launcher=none
```

The empty input is unused: edit the source constants. The program prints
CSV. The regression checks both counts, dimensions, all extents and the
historical volume convention. To describe a bounding box, use `extent`;
to integrate a nonperiodic sampled function, choose an appropriate
quadrature rule explicitly.

Try a grid with one sample in z and observe `dimensionality`. A singleton
axis removes variation along that axis, but its spacing can still represent
a chosen thickness. Dimensionality alone does not decide the physical
units of an integral. Consult the
[domain query definitions](https://github.com/VTT-ProperTune/OpenPFC/blob/master/include/openpfc/kernel/data/domain.hpp)
when adapting a model.

The complete [C++ model](model.cpp) and [starting input](input.json)
are available with this lesson.
